questions.q: What should a values-prod.yaml override file typically contain?
options: Only the keys that differ for production, not a full copy of every key in values.yaml
Nothing — Helm ignores a second values file unless it is a full duplicate of values.yaml
A brand new Chart.yaml for the production environment
The entire Kubernetes manifest for the production Deployment, written out in full
questions.explain: An environment override file holds just what's different — replicaCount, resource sizes, ingress settings — and everything unmentioned falls back to the base values.yaml.

questions.q: In `helm upgrade --install myapp ./myapp --values values.yaml --values values-prod.yaml`, how are the two values files combined?
options: Only the first --values flag is ever read; the second is silently ignored
Helm picks whichever file is alphabetically first
They are merged left to right; the later file's keys win on anything it specifies, everything else falls back to the earlier file
Both files must be byte-for-byte identical or the command fails
questions.explain: Helm merges stacked --values files left to right; later files override matching keys from earlier files, and unspecified keys fall back to the earlier file's values.

questions.q: Which Terraform workflow does Helm's `--values` file stacking most directly parallel?
options: Running terraform init to download a provider plugin
Applying a single resource definition with environment-specific values supplied via terraform apply -var-file
Writing a required_providers block inside a terraform block
Using terraform import to bring an existing resource under management
questions.explain: Both patterns keep one definition (a chart template, a Terraform resource) and supply only the per-environment values through a separate file named explicitly on the command line.

questions.q: What does Helm use in place of a Terraform workspace to keep dev, staging, and prod installs of the same chart from colliding?
options: Nothing is needed — Helm installs are automatically isolated with no extra configuration
A separate Chart.yaml per environment is required, since one chart cannot serve multiple environments
Renaming values.yaml to the environment's name, such as values.yaml.prod
A distinct release name combined with a distinct Kubernetes namespace for each environment's install
questions.explain: Because Helm release state lives in the cluster per release name and namespace, pairing a distinct release name (e.g. myapp-prod) with a distinct --namespace is the practical equivalent of a Terraform workspace isolating state.

questions.q: Where does a Helm release's state (what's installed, with which values) actually live?
options: In a local .tfstate-equivalent file that Helm manages on the developer's own machine
In the cluster itself, tracked per release name and namespace
In the chart's Chart.yaml file, which is rewritten on every upgrade
Helm releases have no persisted state at all
questions.explain: Unlike Terraform's separate state file, a Helm release's state lives inside the cluster, tracked by release name and namespace — which is why release name plus namespace is the isolation mechanism, not a separate state file.
